title: An experiment of double dynamic lighting in an office responding to sky and daylight: Perceived effects on comfort, atmosphere and work engagement
research_question: Can dynamic electrical lighting, complementing and responding to the natural dynamics and qualities of daylight, improve perceived atmosphere and visual comfort in an office environment and thereby improve work engagement?

participants.description: Experimental group: 4 males, mean age 25.5 years, employees of a three-man start-up company and one master's student, working with media production. Control group: 4 participants (3 female, 1 male), mean age 21.5 years, students from Service System Design master's program, working on a semester project. All participants were located in Copenhagen, Denmark and spent more than 70% of their time in front of a computer.
participants.recruitment: open call distribution via the campus intranet

stimuli_or_exposures.description:
An established office space (4.4m x 5m, 2.6m height) at Aalborg University in Copenhagen, Denmark. Walls painted white (77% reflectance), tables (18% reflectance). Two southwest-facing windows (0.8m x 1.07m, 7.7% of floor area) with manually controllable electric blinds. The lighting system consisted of four dimmable and tunable white LED ceiling panels (2700-6500K) and four spotlights (2700-6500K, 36° beam angle, 32° tilt angle).

Dynamic Lighting (Experimental Group): Seven light settings were designed to respond to daylight inflow (50, 200, 350, 500lx) and sky condition (overcast/clear, determined by sky scanner data). Settings varied direct/diffuse ratio (26-40% direct) and CCTs (e.g., 1OC: 2700K direct, 4000K diffuse; Clear sky: 6000K diffuse, 3000K direct; Overcast sky: 4000K diffuse, 3000K direct). Light levels met minimum 500lx on task area and 300lx in surroundings. Lighting changes occurred over 10s every 5 minutes based on sensor data.

Static Lighting (Experimental Group Baseline & Control Group): Traditional diffuse ceiling panels with fixed light levels and CCT (not specified, but implied to be standard office lighting).

measures.construct: Visual comfort (suitability for tasks, discomfort from electrical lighting, discomfort from daylight)
Perceived atmosphere (positive impact on work atmosphere, naturalness of light combo, stimulating for work, comfortable in room)
Work engagement (good work performance, motivated to work, novelty/innovative ideas, concentrated on work, good workflow, willing to take risks)
General lighting experience, visual comfort, work engagement, perceived atmosphere
measures.instrument: Individual in-depth interviews (using reaction cards with 30 adjectives)

mechanisms: Dynamic lighting, by complementing and responding to natural daylight dynamics (variation in direct/diffuse ratio, CCT, intensity, directionality), creates a more natural luminous atmosphere.
This naturalness and variation meet human needs for variation and appreciation, reducing discomfort and supporting engagement.
Specific combinations of warm direct and cool diffuse lighting (or vice versa, depending on sky condition) are perceived as more natural.
Light modelling effects from directional task lighting enhance visual appearance.
Appropriate light levels and CCTs, adjusted dynamically, can support alertness and motivation.
moderators: seasonal changes (low sun angle in December, winter months vs. autumn)
task type (implied by control group difference in creativity)
implementation_implications: Dynamic electrical lighting, complementing daylight, can improve visual comfort, perceived atmosphere, and work engagement in offices.
Design concepts should integrate daylight and electrical lighting, varying direct/diffuse ratio and CCT based on sky conditions and daylight levels.
Future designs should incorporate seasonal changes, time of day, dynamic sunscreens, and individual needs for task lighting as additional dynamic parameters.
Consider visual and non-visual needs in an integrative design approach.
Develop automated systems with user-friendly interfaces for large-scale implementation.
Responsive lighting technology can meet human needs for variation and natural atmospheres.
The current seven light settings could be reduced to five (one for transition/dark hours, two for overcast, two for clear sky) due to low triggering frequency of some settings.
Lower the minimum threshold for triggering daytime settings (e.g., 20-30lx instead of 50lx).
Investigate warmer CCTs and lower intensities for ambient lighting during dark hours, potentially supporting circadian stimuli with low melanotic content.

limitations: Low number of participants (N=4 per group).
Participants were not diverse in age or tasks, limiting generalizability.

Participants sometimes found it difficult to respond to questions regarding their perception of the atmosphere and how it affects their motivation and engagement, leading to long pauses and need for clarifying questions.
Potential for recall bias effects for visual appearance and perceived atmosphere, suggesting a need for more frequent measurement in future studies.
Control group did not work with the exact same subject areas/tasks as the experimental group, potentially influencing outcomes.
The knowledge gained must be considered in relation to other contexts and geographic locations (weather, seasons, daylight inflow, participants, tasks, space may be different).
The duration of lighting change (10s) was not a focus area and not investigated for negative/stimulating effects.
The 4C and 4O light settings were least triggered (2.5%, 0.5%) and not found feasible for future implementations.

The 1OC light setting was triggered 83-88% of the time in November/December, indicating it was used more than intended for transition/dark hours, possibly due to low sun angle and frequent blind usage.

paper_metadata.title: An experiment of double dynamic lighting in an office responding to sky and daylight: Perceived effects on comfort, atmosphere and work engagement
paper_metadata.crossref_title: An experiment of double dynamic lighting in an office responding to sky and daylight: Perceived effects on comfort, atmosphere and work engagement
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The experiment was targeted to develop design strategies and methods by testing the complex interplay between the dynamics of daylight and electrical lighting in an office. The double dynamic lighting design concept is based on the idea of adding task lighting, with a directionality referring to the daylight inflow and a variation on direct/diffuse lighting and respective changes in colour temperature respond to sky conditions and daylight levels. The experiment was conducted in an office space at Aalborg University in Copenhagen from September to December 2019. Four participants moved in and worked in the office with four-week periods of respective standard static lighting as a baseline, and dynamic lighting. In a parallel mixed method approach with interviews and questionnaires, the dynamic lighting was compared to the baseline and to a control group. The results indicate that the dynamic lighting periods had a positive effect on visual comfort, perceived atmosphere and work engagement. The studies helped to develop the definition of five dynamic light settings. Seasonal changes, time of day, dynamic sunscreens and individual needs for task lighting can be implemented in future field experiments as additional dynamic parameters to meet individual needs and circadian potentials for double dynamic light.
